subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Caramelization in the Bean
description: Learn Caramelization in the Bean in one minute.

hook.text: Coffee beans contain 6–9% sugars. When heated above 170°C, these sugars caramelize—literally turning into caramel.

buildup.text: Sucrose breaks down into glucose and fructose, then further into hundreds of aromatic compounds and brown pigments.

discovery.text: Caramelization produces buttery, sweet, and toffee-like notes. It works alongside Maillard reactions to build flavor depth.

twist.text: If roasting goes too far, the sugars burn completely—producing bitter, ashy carbon. Sweetness has a very narrow window.

climax.text: Light roasts preserve more sugars. Dark roasts burn most of them away, replacing sweetness with roast-dominant bitterness.

punchline.text: Sugar meets heat. Go too far and sweetness dies. Precision is everything.

quiz.question: Why do light roasts taste sweeter than dark roasts?
options: Sugar is added to light roasts
Light roasts preserve more natural sugars; dark roasts burn them away

details.summary: Caramelization happens when sucrose and other sugars in the coffee bean break down under heat. This process contributes sweetness, body, and rich brown color. Over-caramelization leads to bitter, burnt flavors that mask the bean's origin character.
details.whyItMatters: Balancing caramelization is what separates a sweet, complex roast from a bitter, ashy one. It is a turning point in every roast profile.
takeaways: Sucrose breaks down into hundreds of caramel compounds
Controlled caramelization adds sweetness and body
Excessive caramelization produces bitterness and carbon notes

faq.question: Which sugars in coffee undergo caramelization during roasting?
faq.answer: Sucrose is the primary sugar that caramelizes during coffee roasting. It begins to break down around 170 degrees Celsius, producing aromatic compounds like furanones that contribute butterscotch and caramel notes.

faq.question: How can a roaster tell when caramelization has gone too far?
faq.answer: Signs include an oily sheen on the bean surface, a sharp smoky smell replacing sweet aromas, and a predominantly bitter, ashy taste in the cupped coffee. Monitoring rate of rise helps prevent this.
